title: Advertising on furniture wagons and Dixieland numbers
summary: Dawson describes how bands advertised dances from wagons, his old maple bass, and Kid Punch.

story.theme_name: Brass bands, parades and jazz funerals
story.community_name: Parading for Mardi Gras and the clubs

blocks.x: At Tom Harris. Well, I guess that's about the same ones, you know. He had a band... That band was operating from Colton. That's the band that was way up in Colton. And he got that job out of Lincoln Beach. And that's a good bass. It's brand new. When I got it... He hadn't used it two years. You like new basses better than old basses? Oh, yeah. I can... I don't know. I like a new instrument. I used to have an old bass. It was called... Maple. It was a pure maple bass. And I used that bass and patched it up in cracks, you know. It'd get cracks in it and have it patched up and sealed in cracks up. And I used that bass a long time before I got this bass. I've been having this one for years now. After I got that cable, I took care of it, you see. I was very careful with it. I had an old bass that I used to use on advertising. You know, a long time ago bands used to go around and advertise, you see. On furniture wagons, you call it. Bands would get out and make advertising. And the trombone and the bass would be right on the tailgate, you see. Right on the back. And we'd stop on from corners, different corners like that. Sometimes we'd have a buck, you see. The kid ran in, run up on. Buddy Puthiel, Kid Punch, some of them. And Kid Punch was in his prime and he had a good band, too, you see. We all have a, what's it called, a buck. And then these kids and things used to run, people used to run around and follow them, their bands, when they advertised. See, like they're gonna have a dance at some club or another, some place or another. The day before that, that dance, they'd advertise for it. That's the way they used to do that. Track level, a little bit of Dixieland numbers. You can't shake, you can't shake like that. Sister Kate and all that, you know, Dixieland numbers. Hot numbers.
I wonder about that. What bands did you play with when you'd be advertising?
